Weekly Wakeup - 08-21-15 - Healthcare licencing and the free market

This is something I mention a lot to my friends, and often get quizzical looks when I talk about private licensing for doctors. They immediately assume that every new doctor joining the system is going to be held to some low standard, and the quality of healthcare will drop dramatically.

However, they seem to not understand the freedom that such a system could potentially bring. If I have a cold and need some antibiotics, I don't need the best doctor in the world to give me a prescription and send me on my way. If I have a serous condition though, I want to get the best medical care I can, but oftentimes it's not obvious just who the best doctor to see is, since they're all held to similar standards.

Private licensing would offer the best of both worlds. If you have a minor illness, and know that you don't need to see the "Mercedes" doctor but are just fine with the "Chevy" doctor, you would be able to save a lot of money. If you have a serious condition though, private licensing gives you the opportunity to determine just exactly who the "Mercedes" doctor is, since you'll be able to see who licensed them.

In my opinion, private licensing could go a long way in the U.S. to increasing the competition among doctors and making healthcare more affordable, and also reducing the ridiculously long wait times for appointments.

Somehow, I doubt there's as much "Mercedes" vs "Chevy" doctors as you think. Some doctors have access to newer technology and methods that haven't become standard across all medical practice yet. Medicine is a deterministic science, with testing protocols and specific methodology. So long as the doctor is adequately trained in that methodology and is smart enough to operate effectively you should be in good hands. It's worth paying attention to when you have a serious condition that could benefit from bleeding edge medicine compared to current standards, but aside from that? Also, you shouldn't get antibiotics for a cold. A cold is a virus, antibiotics will do absolutely nothing to help you and might even give you an antibiotic resistant superbug if you're particularly unlucky. Best to reserve those for confirmed or very likely bacterial infections.

Well put. There are many cases where the "Chevy" doctor would be perfectly adequate. E.g. I've contracted strep throat nearly a dozen times in my lifetime. I am very familiar with the symptoms, and in a free market I'd go into Le Chevy Clinic, have the Chevy doctor or low level nurse do a quick test for strep, and I'd be on my way in ten minutes for a minimal fee.

In the current market, I don't have that option because the AMA guild wants to inflate prices by restricting the supply of doctors.

Not only does licensing restrict the entry pool of doctors, but it also opens the door to suspensions and revoking of licenses to practice medicine. Although there are times where doctors have made wrong decisions and have harmed the patients, the idea of a board of directors deciding if their license gets taken away is scary.

Personally in a free market system where private certifications would be available, i'd hope for a rating system of doctors. Public accessible records and reviews where anyone who files a complaint against a doctor could be read by others choosing who they want to go to. Honestly, the way I've chosen my doctor is by word of mouth. All the glowing reviews he's gotten was the reason I started going to him.

Supposing we got rid of the current model, I'd pick my medical care specialists based on their scientific credentials. Doctors are really just a specific kind of scientist that focuses on organic chemistry and biology specific to human health outcomes.
